policy: Promote only reusable learning. Episode facts remain episode-scoped; rules may be superseded when better evidence appears.

lessons.title: First-found assets are not best-fit evidence
lessons.observed_weakness: Available/open assets were initially treated as attractive production choices before exact use-case requirements were fully defined.
evidence: Generic asset-pack feel persisted after normalization.
Later bespoke/reference-driven passes improved story specificity.
lessons.root_cause: Selection began from available assets rather than from a locked need and comparison set.
lessons.consequence: The renderer optimized around mediocre assets and the visual identity became generic.
lessons.prevention_rule: Define Item requirements before final candidate selection and compare meaningful alternatives.
lessons.detection_method: Decision record must show requirements_locked_before_search and alternatives for important Items.

lessons.title: Normalization cannot fully rescue a generic source asset
lessons.observed_weakness: Palette, hatching, grain and lighting improved coherence but not source-asset specificity.
evidence: V4 remained visibly asset-pack-like despite unified treatment.
lessons.root_cause: Identity and silhouette still came from generic source art.
lessons.prevention_rule: For HERO/PRIMARY visible Items, prioritize bespoke or highly specific source geometry before post-processing.
lessons.detection_method: Ask whether the Item could plausibly belong to many unrelated projects.
implementation_changes: Generic visible asset packs removed from current Living Engraving method

lessons.title: Close-ups require dedicated design quality
lessons.observed_weakness: Zooming a full-body/simple rig into a portrait exposed weak anatomy and facial design.
evidence: Dedicated portrait treatment read stronger than enlarged rig art.
lessons.root_cause: Asset detail level did not match shot scale.
lessons.consequence: Hero close-ups reduced perceived film quality.
lessons.prevention_rule: Treat close-up faces, hands and hero props as their own Items with dedicated references and shot-scale design.
lessons.detection_method: Inspect approval frames at final crop and full delivery resolution before animation.
validation: Close-up approval frame must pass independently

lessons.title: Move expensive texture work to post-processing when possible
lessons.observed_weakness: Complex SVG filters recalculated per object/per frame were unnecessarily expensive.
evidence: Global post-processing preserved the aesthetic idea with lower complexity.
lessons.root_cause: Texture generation was coupled to scene-object rendering.
lessons.prevention_rule: Render clean geometry first, then apply shared texture/film treatment globally where equivalent.
lessons.detection_method: Benchmark per-frame cost before accepting a per-object procedural effect.

lessons.title: Repeated universal transitions create template feel
lessons.observed_weakness: One signature transition reused repeatedly became predictable and decorative.
evidence: Shot-specific hard/light/shadow/match cuts felt more motivated.
lessons.root_cause: Transition choice was treated as global branding rather than edit grammar.
lessons.prevention_rule: Transitions need a shot-specific narrative/editing reason; hard cuts are allowed and often preferable.
lessons.detection_method: Transition review asks why this exact cut exists here.

lessons.title: Scene-level scores hide weak sub-elements
lessons.observed_weakness: Calling Victor, laboratory or apparatus one asset hid weak hands, pose, costume, prop geometry and lighting.
evidence: 62-Item decomposition exposed defects scene-level judgement concealed.
lessons.consequence: Average quality could mask a conspicuous HERO defect.
lessons.prevention_rule: Decompose until independently fail-able/researchable/replaceable elements are separate Items.
lessons.detection_method: Ask whether a subpart could fail while the parent appears acceptable.
validation: Strict final gate operates at Item level

lessons.title: Evidence roles must remain separate
lessons.observed_weakness: A source useful for factual accuracy can have unsuitable image rights or be poor final art.
evidence: Museum/catalog references were strong factual evidence but not always reusable visible assets.
lessons.root_cause: Research source and asset candidate were conflated.
lessons.consequence: Risk of weak selection or rights mistakes.
lessons.prevention_rule: Separate literary, historical, technical, art-direction, rights and asset-candidate roles.
lessons.detection_method: Source registry records roles and visible-asset rights separately.

lessons.title: Source and edition selection must be best-fit and revisable
lessons.observed_weakness: A provisional edition choice risked becoming an unnecessary framework constraint.
evidence: Multiple legitimate editions can have different wording and art-direction implications.
lessons.root_cause: Episode-specific source decision leaked into universal method state.
lessons.consequence: The system could optimize for consistency with an early choice instead of adopting a better later source.
lessons.prevention_rule: Treat source contract as an episode-level best-fit decision; keep it open during development and revalidate dependencies when changed.
lessons.detection_method: Universal method/state must not name a required episode edition; source contract lists candidates and selection status.
implementation_changes: removed designated Frankenstein edition from method state
validation: Strict final may require an explicit contract but never a predetermined edition

lessons.title: A working render is not final artistic approval
lessons.observed_weakness: Reproducible code and successful rendering can create false confidence in unresolved art.
evidence: V5.1 renders correctly while multiple HERO Items remain provisional.
lessons.root_cause: Technical completion and artistic approval were treated as the same milestone.
lessons.consequence: Prototype quality could be mislabeled final.
lessons.prevention_rule: Keep structural and strict-final gates separate.
lessons.detection_method: Structural validator may pass while strict-final remains red until Item/source/continuity gates pass.
validation: Test asserts current prototype cannot pass strict final

lessons.title: Do not score unrendered visual concepts as if they were shot-tested assets
lessons.observed_weakness: Research-qualified design directions can appear numerically 'good' before perspective, crop, motion, lighting and delivery-size behavior have been tested.
evidence: Creature body/head/eye candidates can be ranked on source, period and rights evidence before render, but shot fit/style integration remain unknown until a representative test exists.
lessons.root_cause: Evidence-backed dimensions and empirical shot-performance dimensions were conflated.
lessons.consequence: The system could select a concept that looks strong on paper but fails in the actual film.
lessons.prevention_rule: Before a representative still/motion test, score only dimensions supported by evidence. Leave shot/style/animation performance unapproved until tested in-context.
lessons.detection_method: Candidate status must distinguish RESEARCH_QUALIFIED_NOT_SHOT_TESTED / NOT_MOTION_TESTED from shot-approved states; final selection requires approval-frame or motion-test evidence.
implementation_changes: Creature V5.3 candidate records use research-qualified statuses
No selected candidate is assigned before matched shot tests
validation: Future decision reviews check that shot_fit/style_fit/animation suitability are not claimed as final before test evidence exists.

lessons.title: Publication date is not automatically diegetic design date
lessons.observed_weakness: Costume research began drifting toward 1818/1831 garments because those are the publication editions, even though the frame narrative is dated 17— and the story's world precedes publication.
evidence: Project Gutenberg 1818/1831 texts use 17— dates in Walton's frame.
Surviving 1780s–1790s costume evidence materially changes Victor's plausible silhouette.
lessons.root_cause: Edition time, story time and visual-reference time were conflated.
lessons.consequence: A film can be source-faithful in words while visually placing characters in the wrong era without realizing it.
lessons.prevention_rule: Track diegetic time, publication/edition time and visual-reference time separately. Each Item must state which temporal layer controls its period requirement.
lessons.detection_method: Episode temporal context exists; costume/architecture/technology decisions identify the controlling time layer instead of inheriting publication date.
implementation_changes: Victor costume search expanded to late-18th-century sources
validation: Future historical Item reviews check controlling temporal layer before period scoring

lessons.title: Do not discard high-value source detail merely to keep every visible asset primitive-generated
lessons.observed_weakness: Source-informed exterior and character concepts still looked crude after being rebuilt as simplified Canvas/vector geometry.
evidence: The 1800 Ingolstadt engraving contains dense irregular architecture, bridge, fortification and landmark information that the coded redraw reduced to generic blocks.
Creature and Victor requirements improved, but low-level geometric heads/hands remained visibly constructed in close-up.
lessons.root_cause: Art authoring and film direction were coupled. The renderer was forced to recreate high-information illustration from low-level primitives even when a richer source or bespoke asset could carry that information better.
lessons.consequence: Historical specificity, anatomy and premium illustration quality were lost before cinematography even began.
lessons.prevention_rule: Choose the asset-authoring method per Item. JavaScript may direct and animate a handpicked/reconstructed/bespoke asset instead of redrawing it from primitives. Primitive generation is a candidate method, not a doctrine.
lessons.detection_method: Approval still must be compared against its best reference/candidate. If simplification visibly loses important identity/anatomy/detail, reject the primitive reconstruction and test a higher-information asset method.
implementation_changes: Next experiment adds a bespoke asset-authoring layer before JS compositing
validation: No full V5.3 sequence render until exterior, creature, Victor and apparatus approval stills pass.

lessons.title: Hero assets should not share a crowded source sheet when clean isolation matters
lessons.observed_weakness: A visually strong multi-asset sheet produced overlapping silhouettes and background contamination when individual HERO elements were extracted.
evidence: Creature body and window could be isolated reasonably.
Creature head, Victor and apparatus lost boundaries or inherited neighboring pixels during extraction.
Hair, fingers, cloth edges and engraved linework are precisely the details that HERO animation must preserve.
lessons.root_cause: The source composition optimized for a beautiful collage rather than for independent alpha-safe production assets.
lessons.consequence: Post-isolation cleanup would consume time and can degrade the very detail the higher-quality asset layer was meant to preserve.
lessons.prevention_rule: Generate/acquire HERO assets as individual isolated files with generous transparent margins. Use asset sheets only for ideation, SUPPORT props, or elements whose overlap cannot affect final quality.
lessons.detection_method: Run an isolation/contact-sheet test before accepting any multi-object source. Reject it for HERO use if silhouette, hair, hands, cloth or transparency cannot be recovered cleanly.
implementation_changes: E-VID-005 HERO workflow changed from sheet extraction to one-asset-per-file generation/acquisition.
validation: Each HERO source file must pass alpha-edge inspection and an actual shot composite before selection.

lessons.title: Hero-detail upgrades require supporting-scene simplification or matching detail
lessons.observed_weakness: High-information creature/Victor/apparatus assets looked substantially better than the primitive renderer, but placing them inside the old coded room created a visible detail/style mismatch.
evidence: The first asset-integration contact sheet showed premium engraved figures surrounded by primitive anatomy pages, shelves, skull icon and geometric room dressing.
Removing weak filler and reducing the chamber to window, apparatus, slab, candle, shadow and atmosphere produced a much stronger frame.
lessons.root_cause: Detail hierarchy was inconsistent: HERO assets improved while SUPPORT/environment Items remained below the new quality floor.
lessons.consequence: The shot reads as a collage of high- and low-quality sources even when each HERO asset is strong.
lessons.prevention_rule: When a HERO asset raises the visual ceiling, either raise nearby SUPPORT Items to the same standard or remove/simplify them. Do not preserve weak filler for completeness.
lessons.detection_method: Review the frame at thumbnail and full size; if surrounding objects look visibly cheaper/more generic than the focal asset, simplify or replace them before adding more effects.
implementation_changes: V5.3 chamber rebuilt as a sparse composition around premium assets
Primitive skull/book/anatomy-page clutter removed from the clean test
validation: Clean creation/recoil stills clearly outperform the mixed-detail asset-integration stills.

lessons.title: Choose asset articulation level from the motion the shot actually requires
lessons.observed_weakness: A single flattened high-detail body asset can be transformed convincingly for breathing, tremor, slight lift and camera motion, but cannot produce independent limb articulation without distortion.
evidence: The V5.3 recoil test supports subtle whole-body movement and a cinematic wide shot.
The literary requirement for convulsive limb motion would need independent limb regions, a rig, mesh deformation, or a separate animated asset to be shown clearly.
lessons.root_cause: Static-art quality and motion degrees of freedom are separate requirements.
lessons.consequence: Selecting a beautiful static asset without defining required articulation can force crude warping or under-deliver the action.
lessons.prevention_rule: Before approving a moving Item, define required degrees of freedom. Use a flat asset for rigid/subtle motion; use separated layers/rig/mesh or a dedicated motion asset when independent articulation is narratively visible.
lessons.detection_method: Item motion requirements must specify whether motion is rigid transform, deformable surface, or articulated parts before final asset structure is chosen.
implementation_changes: V5.3 wide creature motion uses restrained rigid/subtle transforms only
True convulsive limb articulation remains unresolved rather than being falsely claimed
validation: Approval motion test documents what the asset can and cannot perform.

lessons.title: Rendering primitives must preserve caller compositing state unless replacement is explicit
lessons.observed_weakness: The eye remained visibly open even when the shot logic set eyelid opacity to zero/closed.
evidence: The ellipse helper assigned ctx.globalAlpha=a internally, overriding the caller's fade alpha.
Passing explicit alpha fixed the shot; changing the helper to multiply parent alpha prevents the same class of bug elsewhere.
lessons.root_cause: A low-level drawing primitive silently replaced caller compositing state instead of composing with it.
lessons.consequence: Animation logic can appear artistically wrong even when timing/state variables are correct.
lessons.prevention_rule: Reusable rendering primitives should multiply/compose with inherited opacity by default. Any primitive that intentionally resets alpha/composite state must document that contract.
lessons.detection_method: Renderer contract test asserts the ellipse primitive multiplies parent globalAlpha; motion lookdev includes start/mid/end state frames for opacity-driven reveals.
implementation_changes: Changed canonical ell() helper from ctx.globalAlpha=a to ctx.globalAlpha*=a
validation: First-eye matched frames now show closed -> partial -> open without a false yellow iris in the closed state.
